0003917d82f19db1.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in an area with seed-bearing plants, dandelions, grasses, trees with fallen seeds or acorns.

00b53e2a91fbdf4c.text: Then Leave it to thaw. Continuity. Will it still be frozen tomorrow? Observation as care. Walk back.

00cffe456be834c1.text: The idea to carry. Flowers are bright on purpose. Their colour is an advertisement, calling pollinators in to feed.

00def100471f43ce.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best after leaf fall when tree structures are fully visible.

011b40a9713741be.text: Then Step into shadow. Shadow is a microclimate. Temperature, moisture, light all change in a few steps.

016dfcbf4b4fc691.text: Four words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

01c21c6f6293b634.text: Why it matters. Conkers come from horse chestnut trees, and acorns come from oak trees: a simple, useful fact if children ask which tree their seed came from.

023be85c99561588.text: Before you go out. Two things to gather.

0271de97b2739055.text: Why it matters. Most of the animals children choose to mask, fox, owl, hedgehog, badger, are common in gardens and hedgerows in the UK, so this is a natural link to a short talk about nocturnal and daytime animals.

032e09abedda88a2.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Works in any outdoor space, the point is that life is everywhere.

0410582cf09b2dd2.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Identify safe areas to look, log piles, leaf litter, wall cracks. Brief the class: look but do not lift or disturb.

042e98e11ef4743b.text: Before you go out. Two things to gather. Walk your hedge or your trees the day before and see what is down. If nothing has fallen yet, a bag of conkers, acorns or sycamore keys from a park does the same job.

042f4bf8a2fca16d.text: Birds. Which birds stayed, and what are they doing?

050cfa3a907f2a31.text: Colours. Which colours are leaving, and which are arriving?

05aeed203fccefc9.text: Why it matters. A child who is told it is autumn learns a word. A child who finds autumn, in a colder railing or a yellowing leaf, learns that looking works. That confidence is the foundation for every investigation that follows.

05e99aacaefc20da.text: What it is for. About what flowers are in your green space and how they got there. The skill is looking, smelling and touching.

062231d271216db9.text: Why it matters. A feeder is the winter birds lesson answered with the hands: the children who stood still and counted the birds now give them something.

0647e70da9345d3a.text: The idea to carry. Children count everything alive within ten steps of where they stand, then begin to work out what makes something living: breathing, growing, reproducing, dying.

076ed56dfd6a33dc.text: Why it matters. Watching an animal work turns a distant creature into a neighbour with a job to do. It builds observation, patience, and empathy: children start to feel what a bird's day of nest-building might be like.

07dffdea71e7be8b.text: Why it matters. Looking closely is a skill, and most children glance rather than see. Discovering that a single colour holds many shades sharpens attention and delights them.

0800c508935dcbd3.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Summer produces strong natural scents everywhere.

08415080c3abb341.text: Then Put it back. Same closing as Spring's Underground practice. The earth holds us. Walk back.

08a5da992f63367b.text: Then Greet the spring. Close the winter season with hope. The cycle continues. Walk back together.

08ab8b34a97ff4bd.text: Then Meet the trees. Take the class to four or five different trees around the grounds. Model the slow flat-hand touch yourself before the children scatter. Name the trees casually as hands land on them.

0914250d79ac6448.text: Why it matters. We tend to think an outdoor space is mostly empty, with a bit of nature dotted about.

0920beadfaab329f.text: The idea to carry. The garden becomes a kitchen. Children identify what is edible and which part of the plant it is, then wash, tear, cut and mix a simple seasonal dish with child-safe tools.

0a6f69da558ab6d2.text: And finish in Circle. Build observation skills. Migration vs residency. Science connection. Beautiful question. Handle with care.

0b68ff46d11ee8c7.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Check the day before that there are conkers or acorns on the ground. Bring one of each to show indoors if you can.

0b7b9181773da7e1.text: The idea to carry. Children sketch a design for a bird feeder, then build a simple version from a recycled plastic bottle, before taking it outside to hang it on site. Indoors first: what birds struggle to find in winter, and how we could help.

0bd0c39ac32e1de3.text: Then The decomposer hunt. Damp and dark is where the crew works, so send the hunt there. Every find gets the same question: what do you think it eats? The answer, dead stuff, is the whole lesson arriving by itself.

0c52634c3048e4ff.text: Why it matters. Falling leaves give young children a gentle, visible way to meet the idea of endings. Nothing is lost here: a fallen leaf is on its way to becoming soil that feeds next year's growth.

0c5b52258395ea2e.text: And finish in Circle. Compare surfaces: stone, metal, wood, soil. Shadow, under a tree, near water. Opens up ecology, food chains, gratitude.

0cd240abb219f265.text: Then Stand with your green. Let them choose. No wrong answer. Dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen.

0cf4890ed96b42a6.text: The idea to carry. Autumn is the most visible season: leaves turn and fall, air cools, rain and wind pick up, plants die back and animals change what they do. This first session does not teach any of that.

0de57a54c4b39200.text: Why it matters. Minibeasts are the easiest wild animals for children to meet up close. Handling them gently is a first lesson in respect for living things: gentle hands, quiet voices, and everything goes back exactly where it was found.

0ec302dd17f20df6.text: Then Clue hunt. Nothing gets lifted or poked. A sleeping hedgehog woken in winter can die of it, so the rule is look and leave.

0ee662384f33b3a3.text: Why it matters. Making art with found nature asks children to look twice: once at the leaf, once at the world. The picture is theirs; the materials belong to the place.

1155e74795849ec8.text: Then Welcome it. Acknowledgment. The bird doesn't need our thanks, but saying it changes us. Walk back.

11d99f5266ce771b.text: Why it matters. Freezing is one of the first big changes a young child can see, touch and understand with their own hands. It shows that the same stuff can take different forms.

1212f521088ba7b7.text: Earth, air and water. What is changing the garden: earth, air or water?

136593d7b8029ddc.text: And finish with Circle and feedback. Combine everyone's totals on the board into one big class tally chart. Conkers and acorns fall straight down and roll, so they gather under their own tree. That is why one tree gives so many.

13961334c379a98c.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Scout a corner that can honestly stay untidy through winter, and clear it with whoever manages the site: a habitat that gets tidied away in November teaches the wrong lesson twice.

13ddb2566773e97d.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Walk the space yourself the day before and find three changes worth being led to: a tree turning, a patch of fallen leaves, a plant dying back. You will not point them out; you will steer the wander past them.

14146f57394168db.text: The idea to carry. Wildflowers spread themselves. Seeds travel on the wind, stick to animal fur, hitchhike in bird droppings, float on water, or get carried by people. Every wildflower in your school grounds got there somehow — and children become detectives investigating how.

14c7ebf9e28e532a.text: What it is for. Connect the season's discoveries into one cycle, and see that people are part of the garden's system. The skill is connecting ideas.

154f7847523814a5.text: Then Open the case file. Hand out the journals with some ceremony: this is a detective's case file, and it will be kept all term. Date the first page together.

156c063ef74d3367.text: Why it matters. Where does a fallen leaf go is a question a five-year-old can investigate to the end, on the ground under their own feet.

15b0ad4047b71e50.text: How it runs. You start with Listen for what's new. Give them 30 seconds of silence first. Then ask them to open their eyes and walk slowly, looking for anything that feels new or awake.

15bf9ca142c8439c.text: How it runs. You start with Find the darkest spot. Under hedges, behind buildings, in corners. Shadow creates habitat.

15d9474cdafa8555.text: Then Wonder. A moment of wonder. Some kids will find this mind-blowing.

16223b4343f94bec.text: Then Make. Work in partners to make bird feeder: halve an orange (teacher halves them ahead of time), scoop out the flesh, tie string to 2 sides to make a hanging basket, fill with birdseed, hang on trees in the school grounds.

16c5a8b9507b0243.text: Then Look. Three places to look, in this order: the hedge and low branches, the ground under them, then the sky. Keep the group in one slow line rather than a rush. Binoculars go to whoever has found something, not whoever asks.

17b0e1b56a318989.text: What it is for. Most creatures left or hid. But the birds stayed. Children find a winter bird, watch it work, and reflect on what it means to stay when things are hard. The skill is looking and listening.

17be9306ec15f5c5.text: Then Gather the ingredients. Restate the two safety rules while hands are still empty: fallen only, and potions are for looking, never drinking. Said now, once, cheerfully, they hold all session.

183b1984f3442b91.text: And finish with Circle and feedback. Size, weight and shape.

1902995f1cbfbf79.text: Seed bombs. Spreading wildflowers for pollinating insects.

195d26368e28f4b7.text: Then Lift. Lift, look, and put back exactly as you found it. Two hands under a log, rolled towards them so nothing runs over their fingers.

19eb8649ac657045.text: What it is for. Investigate where seeds are on plants and test how each seed travels. The skill is wondering how.

1a0e7542be97a483.text: Then Alive. Let them argue. A fallen leaf, a seed, moss on a wall: alive or not? The wondering is the learning.

1ae6078490c9a5de.text: What it is for. Back after summer. The land didn't wait. Children explore what changed while they were away: what grew, what died, what moved. A practice about time and continuity. The skill is looking and smelling.

1b19cb86c853751c.text: Then Warm your hands. Generosity of warmth. Touch a cold railing, a frozen bench. You give warmth. Walk back.

1b98f7e215739877.text: And finish in Circle time. Size, weight and shape.

1bc57a15fd6a169d.text: The idea to carry. When the air gets cold enough, water freezes. A puddle turns to hard ice, dew on the grass becomes white frost, and mud sets solid.

1c6fbbd9bfd3d81a.text: Then Trace a branch. The architecture of a tree. In summer it's hidden by leaves. Now you can see the whole structure.

1c9a2edc002a8561.text: Green. How many different greens can you find?

1cdf241bc1ff4ca1.text: Then Tuck it in. Push an acorn into soft earth. Walk back.

1d182c238ea5433c.text: How it runs. You start with Look at the soil. Not just "dirt." Leaves, twigs, stones, sand, clay, roots, insects. It's a whole world.

1d27e9a02e8f8dd6.text: The last warmth. Where can you still find warmth?

1d3d8a05e1b282aa.text: Then Take outside. Only leaves that have already fallen. Aim for at least thirty as a class. Back inside, remind them to follow the template lines when cutting. Keep the animal photos on display. Make suggestions, then give them time to be creative.

1d5eae8da503cae2.text: Then Thank what you found. Model this. Bow slightly, say Thank you, little bud. Kids will follow. Some will giggle. That's fine. The gesture still lands. Then walk back together in quiet.

1dcd820d1ae9fd9f.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Find areas with strong shadow contrast, north-facing walls, dense hedges, under evergreens.

1de66d8587eebfc1.text: The idea to carry. Local birds eat what the land gives them — seeds, insects, worms, berries. In winter and early spring food is scarce. Children make a simple bird feeder from half an orange and birdseed, then hang it in the school grounds.

1f07b791179ebdc7.text: What it is for. Observe and identify common garden birds using a simple spotter sheet. The skill is looking and listening.

1f0bf411914828d7.text: Why it matters. A child who has stood still for a whole minute and heard three different birds has done real science: noticed, counted, and asked what is there.

1fa644bd262c6e90.text: Then Explore. Let children explore flowers and pollinators in the space. Look for bees, butterflies, hoverflies. Which flowers are they visiting? Are there flowers with no visitors?

1fc28fc1eb7a03f6.text: What it is for. Children search for things that are opening: buds, flowers, cracks where green pushes through. A practice about beginnings and the courage of new growth. The skill is looking, smelling and touching.

20466c58bf30cf1a.text: The idea to carry. Children walk among the trees of their outside space and talk about why trees matter: for the air we breathe and for the creatures that live in and around them.

2047f5dd770aef2d.text: Why it matters. Pollinators carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds and fruit. A great deal of the food we eat depends on them.

22b6211036197ddd.text: Then Hold it. Weight, texture, shape. A whole tree fits in an acorn.

2401c88780385b2c.text: Then Collect. Seeds from the ground only. Nothing pulled off a living plant.

246698754641cb91.text: Then Wonder. The abundance of life is the summer lesson. We are surrounded.

247f8691305abfd0.text: Then Earth: what the ground holds. The dark crumbly layer is the whole of session four in miniature. Do not explain it yet; just make sure hands meet it. Everything dug up goes back: the patch should look undisturbed when you leave.

24bb8ad04f4ebc19.text: Two words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

25e7f68502fd1731.text: Then Name your green. Calm green. Electric green. Sleepy green. Let them be creative.

275f28de1dfc03de.text: The idea to carry. Wind is air that is moving, and children can feel it long before they can explain it.

27c0103d1a3e1e9a.text: Then Us. Same problem, same four answers. Coats and a full cupboard are storing. The lights going on earlier is the light going. Let them find the parallels.

27d129dd43a13585.text: How it runs. You start with Find a seed. Dandelion seeds, acorns, berries, grass seeds. Anything that carries the next generation.

2842cf6576384bd4.text: Why it matters. Children often assume plants grow because someone planted them. Learning that wildflowers spread themselves, in surprising ways, changes how children see the world. A dandelion is not a weed — it is a flower that found its own way here.

28a3d1f5526f83a9.text: Then Wonder. Joy, energy, not wanting to go to bed. All valid. This connects to seasonal rhythms.

28cc9ab3a5610899.text: Then Collect. Seeds from the ground, or ones that come away at a touch. Nothing pulled off a living plant.

2943a2a3a822e57d.text: Then Wonder. Gentle. Not scary. Some children fear darkness. This reframes it as a place where things thrive.

2a46118cddc89400.text: Then Make. An adult cuts a small hole in each clean bottle, a few centimetres up from the base. Children never handle the knife.

2a83b4688fc5cbc1.text: Why it matters. Tracks are proof that children share their space with animals they hardly ever see. Following that clue builds observation, careful looking, and a kind of gentle detective thinking, working out a story from what was left behind.

2aea9ddf7c430740.text: Then Wonder. Reframing the schoolyard as a living food web. Some kids will find this exciting.

2b34303e86d54467.text: What it is for. Water becomes something entirely different just from cold. Children find frozen things, touch ice, and reflect on transformation: how something can change completely and still be itself. The skill is touching and looking.

2b5e57ade1ac52ca.text: Wildflower investigation. What flowers are in your green space and how did they get there?

2d509014a1a7b0c6.text: Why it matters. Wind is one of the first invisible forces a young child meets. Learning to read it by its effects, the grass bending, a leaf tumbling, is early science and early wonder at once.

2db4c3ab1d2ed631.text: What it is for. Collect, sort, count and compare conkers and acorns as a hands-on measuring and data activity. The skill is sorting and comparing.

2e43f6457799ef7b.text: Then Stand with each one. Slow looking. 30 seconds per thing. Notice detail.

2e988a0a82022d4c.text: The idea to carry. Soil is not just dirt. It is a whole world made of broken-down leaves, tiny stones, sand, clay, roots and small living things, all mixed together.

2e9cdd6f3ab2db04.text: The idea to carry. Bark is a tree's coat, and every kind of tree wears its own. In this session children meet the trees a new way: not with their eyes first, but with their hands.

2f84dadf442b6df8.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Works anywhere there is vegetation, even a single tree or patch of grass.

305aea9abdf6a854.text: Then Take a rubbing. Hand out paper and crayons at the trees, not before: paper in the hand turns walkers into runners. Pairs work well, one holds the paper flat, one rubs, then swap. Slow strokes beat hard pressing: say gently, like stroking a cat.

31d0244eb8eaec3c.text: How it runs. You start with Settle. If your grounds have few trees, walk the candidates yourself beforehand and steer the choosing between two or three. The children still make the choice; you set the shortlist.

31df8ad801aba4af.text: Before you go out. Nothing to bring. Walk out as you are.

3215f6e47e028bc0.text: Then Listen. Wind in branches, a robin, distant traffic, crunching leaves underfoot. The autumn orchestra is smaller but still playing.

3221407eee811dc4.text: Then Wonder. Colour preference reveals something personal. Light touch.

32945290fd5f8420.text: How it runs. You start with Find a food source. Everything is food for something. Leaves for caterpillars, seeds for birds, nectar for bees, bark for beetles.

32e063a9dd0fd279.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Scout for areas with visible buds, flowers, or new growth. Any green space will have something opening in spring.

334668ddee26b4a6.text: Then Letting go. Find the stalk end. There is a small clean scar where the leaf joined the branch. The tree built that. It let go on purpose.

336f0df3a8c0b015.text: Smell. What is the strongest smell you can find?

33819d1e69eafed4.text: Then Engage. Allow children to raise their hands to give feedback.

33d284815048c1d1.text: And finish in Circle. Introduce the idea of nature's recycling system: the leaf falls, the creatures break it down, the soil gets the goodness, a new plant grows.

343d3ace1bf6bef9.text: The idea to carry. Warm air carries scent, so summer is the richest season for smells: cut grass, warm soil, flowers, herbs, rain on hot ground.

34c8abae591d6a22.text: Then Introduce. Robin, blackbird, pigeon, gull, crow, blue tit, sparrow. Every answer goes on the list, and a made-up bird gets a kind no. Hand out the spotter sheets and quickly point out two or three of the pictures on it.

34e18d2adb76a748.text: Why it matters. Seeds travel in four main ways. Wind: dandelion, sycamore helicopters. Animals: burrs stick to fur, berries are eaten and the seeds pass through. Water: some seeds float, a coconut for one.

35119b53f9cafe05.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. This works in any outdoor space where living things can be found.

351916caedbe1064.text: And finish in Circle. Let children share their count and describe what they found. Wind, birds, previous plantings, nature finding a way. Connects to the seed bomb practice and forward thinking about stewardship. After, for you: You investigated the hidden life in your school grounds.

3547726100075218.text: How it runs. You start with Feel what's underground. Let them feel the earth. Damp? Warm? Cool? Moving?

35e433916037aa68.text: Then Thank the workers. Whisper it. Bees don't care, but the children will remember saying it.

3632a3c0f7dbaa50.text: How it runs. You start with Find. Set the boundary first: this hedge, this tree, this patch of ground. Pairs work well, one tray between them.

365a00c2280fdd74.text: Dark. What grows in the darkest spot you can find?

36b92007a87b7706.text: What it is for. Find the birds that live in our grounds in winter, by listening first and looking second. The skill is looking and listening.

36c4f447e47911c8.text: Then The harvest. The nothing-goes-in-mouths-yet rule holds through the harvest: eating waits for clean hands and the table.

38f07b120e4fc4c4.text: Then Keep the scent. Anchoring the memory. Walk back breathing slowly.

394384ddb014d135.text: The idea to carry. Children collect leaves outside and glue them into patterns and pictures on A5 paper, taking influence from what they can see around them.

398f13fca83d69cf.text: Then Collect. Only leaves that have already fallen. Nothing picked from a living plant. Collect at least thirty as a class. Better too many than not enough.

39e47c732c2ee218.text: What it is for. Make an animal mask using nature and begin to tell a story about your chosen animal. The skill is telling a story.

39f21d23c040864d.text: How it runs. You start with Find something falling. Autumn is the season of release. Let them find their own examples. Don't direct too much.

3a37ea8541d0b86d.text: Then Wonder. This connects warmth to nourishment. Kids might say "nice" or "relaxed". All good.

3a875827085bd6f4.text: And finish with The scraps go home. Walk the scrap bowl to the compost together and add it as green material with a handful of brown on top.

3bb46caf33dd53a5.text: Then Greet. Tie the wool loosely; it must never bite the bark, and take it home at the end of the year. Write the chosen name down where the class can see it back inside.

3cdd1dffe1def2e8.text: How it runs. You start with Find three living things. Tree, flower, bird, insect, grass, moss. Anything alive. Three is enough.

3d8846c05bf46665.text: Then Build the big circle. Let the children place the pieces and argue the joins; wrong placements that get corrected by their neighbours are the thinking happening out loud. The one join worth insisting on if nobody finds it: where do people go?

3d94d024635bd907.text: Then Thank the wind. Face into the wind for the thank you. Walk back.

3d9aae28fdedff92.text: Three words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

3dece0c1fa5fe160.text: Then Air: hunting the wind. The sleeping ribbon matters as much as the dancing one: sheltered and exposed is exactly the distinction the animals need in session seven. Name the still places warmly: this is where you would put a nest.

3e39abf20d068a84.text: The idea to carry. Children collect a variety of leaves outside to create an animal mask they can wear, then show it and tell a story about their chosen animal. One session, three hats.

3ede44dddaf7b3c9.text: Warmth. What has the sun been warming?

3ee2c5f8d44cb580.text: And finish in Circle. Let a few children hold their evidence up for the whole circle. Hedgehogs, bats, some butterflies behind the shed. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer. Longer, until midwinter, and then it starts coming back. Big guesses welcome.

3f23386be9588e50.text: Then Wonder. Transformation metaphor. Temperature changed water. What changes us?

3f716f7216b77cbd.text: The idea to carry. Children hunt for minibeasts in soil, under logs and in bushes, look closely at legs, wings and homes, and learn that every creature has a special role.

3f7784e2412026a2.text: First signs. What can you find that is waking up?

3ffaf3226fb640a9.text: And finish in Circle. Shape, colour, size, smell. Descriptive language lives here. Back to the earth. Nothing in nature is wasted.

401947e41593f0e0.text: Leaves and their trees. Which tree did your leaf come from?

40505ba9173b52a7.text: Then Explore. Give children 10 minutes to explore their outdoor space, using only their senses.

40704c83bea161f5.text: Then Measure a shadow. Shadow length changes through the day and the year. They're measuring the earth's tilt with their feet.

408599e4e21cd2e0.text: And finish in Circle. Compare spots. Why was one cooler than another? Trees, buildings, walls: nature vs human-made. Animals, insects, plants. Shade is shared.

414b94f5e6bd79e6.text: Then Thank the shade. A hand on the trunk. A pat on the grass. Walk back together.

4154be51316f93ff.text: How it runs. You start with Find the loudest colour. Flowers compete for attention, from pollinators. The brightest colour is the loudest shout.

41807632614e7ec2.text: Before you go out. Six things to gather. Print the mask template, one per child. Have a few photos of common animals ready to show: fox, hedgehog, owl, robin.

42533376f9142d4b.text: How it runs. You start with Talk. Discussion about art in nature: patterns, colours, shapes, textures. Nature is full of art that nobody designed. Today we use what nature gives us to make our own.

426e1ca4c4b4f11e.text: Before you go out. Five things to gather. Decide the dish by what is actually ready: a chopped fruit salad, a leaf-and-crunch salad, or simply apples cut and shared count fully. Check allergies before the session. Wash produce beforehand if your water access outside is limited.

438d07ee059a494a.text: The idea to carry. Children walk under the turning trees, bring back one fallen leaf each, lay them out from greenest to brownest, and work out that the tree is taking its green back in before winter and the other colours were there all along.

441a8e59d688b6ee.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a day with some breeze. If calm, look for any air movement, thermals near walls, drafts.

445867d64825dc47.text: What it is for. Find out what happens to a leaf after it falls, and meet the creatures that help it break down. The skill is looking closely.

44c986a7255fd134.text: Why it matters. Watching one bird do its work is a gateway to paying attention to everything. It builds patience and slow looking, which children get few chances to practise.

44db13e5ea0fcfd2.text: The idea to carry. The sun warms us directly, on our skin, and it warms the things around us: walls, stones, soil, bark. Some surfaces hold that heat and stay warm long after the sun has moved.

451dbd82facb64e1.text: Why it matters. Most children can't name three local birds. Paying attention to birds is a gateway to paying attention to everything. A bird feeder is a tiny act of care that pays back immediately — birds arrive within hours.

45200969081cdd18.text: Why it matters. Children live mostly indoors and rarely notice the turn of the seasons. Slowing down to find the first signs of spring builds patient attention and a felt sense that they are part of a living, changing world.

453c3b3c97e67f11.text: Then Appreciate. Allow your class to go back to a spot in your grounds to thank the minibeasts.

4554c63d26e11dc7.text: And finish in Circle. Share hiding spots: under logs, leaf piles, walls. Warmth, shelter, safety, dryness. Design thinking. Fun question. Connects to seasonal preference.

4650b846ee04161d.text: The idea to carry. We call it all green, but green is really dozens of different shades: dark moss, bright new leaf, pale lichen, deep emerald grass. This is a perception practice.

4663d3ed87b27c84.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a sunny day. If overcast, focus on warm surfaces and sheltered spots.

46bf2849b9578171.text: And finish in Circle. Circle time for reflection on what they have learnt, highlighting importance of wildflowers. Connect back to the discussion. Without wildflowers, pollinators lose food sources. Give them a moment to think about their local area.

46e2af1fe923c0cb.text: Then Wonder. The seasonal cycle as a comfort. Winter is not forever.

4738e0011b9728c1.text: The idea to carry. Children mark where their own shadow ends, hunt for the evidence of animals and plants preparing for the cold, and sort what they find into the four answers to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground.

474d8b9e073d26a0.text: What it is for. Flowers compete for attention. Children find the loudest colour, look inside a flower, and discover the hidden world of pollen, patterns, and tiny structures. The skill is looking and smelling.

47b740654f31bf94.text: Then Touch the water. Let them get their hands wet. Sensory experience matters more than staying clean.

47c4d67735705ede.text: Then Touch the ice. Sharp, smooth, brittle, stinging. Ice is water doing something extraordinary.

47db92fb157d520a.text: The idea to carry. This is the first session back after summer. While the class was away, the grounds carried on: plants grew taller, some flowers finished, seeds set, spiders moved in.

47e665630fd3bde0.text: Then Discuss. No wrong answers. If nobody says the trees, point at one. Keep it simple: after a leaf falls it slowly breaks down, with help from some friendly garden creatures. Worms, woodlice, centipedes. They eat parts of the leaf.

47f264399932d07a.text: Then Say thank you. Thank you, oak tree. Thank you, robin. Thank you, moss. Model this first. It will feel awkward and then wonderful.

4868b9e65e869cf6.text: The idea to carry. Children learn three winter survival strategies, hibernate, migrate and adapt, take a short clue hunt outside, then sort animal picture cards into the correct group.

4881afc54f5e2cfb.text: How it runs. You start with Talk. Spend about 10 minutes on this. Talk about the importance of flowers and the process of pollination. Use simple language: bees visit flowers for food (nectar), and while they visit they carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps new flowers grow.

48849606f999b306.text: Then Wonder. Decomposition as transformation. The leaf became the soil the seed grows in.

489d54247b6d1e39.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Bring a stone per pair, or chalk if your ground is hard. Go out at the time of day you could come back at, so the shadows can be put side by side later. Nothing else.

48ffc34174a643e0.text: Then Reflect. Reflection on how the colours and pigments of nature come out on the page. How it feels to use nature creatively. The colours are softer, more varied, more surprising than shop-bought paint.

4937f149191fcaa3.text: And finish in Circle. Moss, damp, insects, hiding spots. Different, cooler, quieter, maybe a bit scary. All valid. Science connection: shade-loving plants, mushrooms, ferns.

49ccc55b46d1721b.text: Before you go out. Two things to gather. Print or draw six to eight animal cards: a hedgehog, a dormouse, a bat, a swallow, a house martin, a robin, a blackbird, a squirrel. Big enough to sort on the floor.

4a2c678f21bb5030.text: Then Wonder. Metaphor territory. Some kids will get it, some won't. Both fine.

4a8e5393f28b61f7.text: Our Earth's magnificent trees. Why are trees so important for our existence?

4ab6f5a52311f1fb.text: And finish in Circle. Some children will whisper it to themselves. That counts.

4b7a359ece825e3c.text: And finish in Circle. Nests, structures, the sky. Drawing opportunity: sketch the branch pattern. Personal connection to dormancy.

4b8136efecd29f1e.text: What it is for. Notice and name the changes autumn has made to the garden, using all the senses. The skill is noticing change.

4b8e5f8a138b63ea.text: The idea to carry. In winter, deciduous trees drop their leaves and stand bare. Suddenly you can see the whole shape of a tree: the trunk, the branches splitting into smaller and smaller twigs, and the sky behind them.

4bb96b813314e418.text: Why it matters. Smell is the sense we teach children the least, yet it is the one most tied to memory and feeling.

4be19b7d7c968008.text: Then The colour line. Lay every leaf on the ground in one long line, greenest at one end, brownest at the other. Let the class argue about where each one goes.

4be360244b2b2308.text: Why it matters. Eight sessions of separate wonders become one understanding here: the garden is a system, everything in it is used again, and people, who ate from it, composted into it and built homes for its animals, are inside the circle, not outside it.

4c10424d4445083d.text: Then Look inside a flower. Pollen, patterns, tiny hairs, colour gradients. The inside of a flower is a world.

4c18334e0c879409.text: Why it matters. A child who has thanked a tree treats trees differently. This session turns the biggest living things on the school grounds from scenery into neighbours.

4ca2e7a49900a1f4.text: The idea to carry. Children lift the fallen leaves to meet the woodlice, worms and fungus threads eating them, dig down to the layer where leaves stop looking like leaves, and find that it has become soil.

4d3c95cc1e225547.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a warm day when the contrast between sun and shade is noticeable.

4dec565cd626ad01.text: Everything is connected. How is everything we explored connected?

4e2e9b1571d7b038.text: Then What a seed carries. Four things they can look for in anything they pick up. Try them on an acorn, a sycamore key, a conker, a blackberry.

4ec41167a15ad49b.text: Then Say see you. Close the autumn season. Walk back slowly.

4fc3dc9c34c6eea9.text: What it is for. Summer days are the longest. Children trace the sun's arc, play with shadows, and reflect on what long light means for the land and for themselves. The skill is noticing by looking.

4fe3625bdd63c736.text: The idea to carry. Winter is the easiest time of year to see birds: the leaves are down, so the hedge and the trees hide nothing, and the birds that stay all year are busy finding food in the short days.

5173ccf33ef093a5.text: Then Wonder. We share space with creatures we rarely see. The tracks are proof.

5284b6f39d420689.text: Then Walk. Bark, leaves, height, shape. How many different trees can the class spot?

529c49de7f4a403f.text: Why it matters. Decomposers (fungi and bacteria) and detritivores (worms, woodlice, centipedes) work together to break down dead material. Detritivores shred it into smaller pieces, and decomposers break it down further.

52e88187e6afd612.text: How it runs. You start with Collect. Ask children to gather fallen leaves and petals from the ground — ones that have already fallen.

52f08e9da78ae67d.text: How it runs. You start with Find the last warmth. A sun-warmed bench, a sheltered corner, warm bark, their own hands in pockets. The warmth is retreating.

535619528aa7a747.text: Why it matters. The autumn colour change is one of the most beautiful slow things a child can watch, and it is happening on a schedule no one controls.

5384a6c30f08abbd.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Scout for early spring signs, swelling buds, snowdrops, longer daylight. Best in late February.

539f120689152d26.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a frosty morning. If no frost, focus on the coldest surfaces and visible breath.

53fb6e1bffe10d5c.text: The idea to carry. As autumn deepens, the soundscape thins out. Many birds have stopped their spring song, insects have gone quiet, and the busy hum of summer fades.

54055c196ec96edd.text: What it is for. Winter days are short and shadows are long. Children step into the darkest spots and discover that moss, ferns, and quiet things thrive in shade. A practice about finding life in the dark. The skill is noticing by looking.

5419b0c50b09aa64.text: Return. What changed while we were away?

541a15b87cfb46d1.text: And finish in Circle time. Come back in a week and count who is using it. That count is the evaluation the design and technology link asks for.

5489eb55983f828b.text: How it runs. You start with Shadow. This one needs sun. If the sky is flat grey, say so honestly, go straight to the hunt, and mark the shadows on the first bright day instead.

54e24fd0937c36e7.text: The idea to carry. Children collect conkers and acorns from the school grounds, then sort, count and compare them using simple maths skills. Introduce indoors, collect and sort outside, then a circle to total everyone's finds in one class tally chart.

54e37f0ab1c705b1.text: And finish in Circle. Compare body parts and locations. Make a class list of everything wind touched. Geography, weather, imagination.

566665e2febe6850.text: And finish in Circle. Compare different spots: some sandy, some clay, some leafy. Earthy, musty, damp, alive. Build vocabulary. Connects to food, life, everything.

5687128febef5f64.text: What it is for. Discover the different ways animals prepare for winter, and improve the garden as a winter home. The skill is caring for wildlife.

56f981b513aca56c.text: What it is for. Understand simply why wildlife needs extra help in winter, and the three main ways animals survive the cold. The skill is sorting and reasoning.

57322b39087a96c6.text: And finish in Circle. Greens fading. Gold, amber, crimson, brown. Science connection: chlorophyll, sugars, light.

5793af92d085ca18.text: Then Watch a bird. Winter birds work hard. Every moment is about finding enough to eat. Observe for 2 minutes.

579ca60e58cee93f.text: Then Identify. Bring the class back to the circle. Let them discuss in partners or raise their hands.

57e011d3bdf0d6d6.text: Then Wonder. This is deep for younger kids. Keep it light. Older KS2 can handle the depth. Follow their lead.

57f144dcc3e49a72.text: What it is for. Winter mud and frost reveal who else has been here. Children become detectives: reading tracks, comparing prints, and discovering they share this space with creatures they rarely see. The skill is looking and touching.

57f6d28554d3beac.text: Then Leave your mark. Adding our mark to the record. Walk back.

58081583177716d0.text: How it runs. You start with Feel the wind. One cheek, the back of the neck, through their hair. Wind has direction and intention.

58478ef3616240f7.text: Then Wonder. Resilience. Some kids will connect this to their own experiences. Let them.

586d523ffa4156dc.text: Then Thank the quiet. Walk back in silence. See how long the class can hold it.

5882b4b794ee7638.text: Then Chase a smell. Crush a leaf gently between fingers. Sniff bark. Get close to flowers. Hands-on smelling.

5892b31afe2fe47a.text: Why it matters. Opening is a beautiful, slow thing that children usually miss because it happens on nature's time, not theirs. Watching a bud unfold teaches patience and wonder, and the idea that new beginnings take a kind of quiet bravery.

58a82353107c2ed3.text: Then Thank the colours. Autumn colour is brief and brilliant. Gratitude for impermanence.

58add56ece0082ce.text: Then Create. Gather the children back inside. Let them take their time with this.

58f0f6d39d3d9fa4.text: The idea to carry. Seed bombs are little balls of clay packed with wildflower seeds. Children roll them up in class, then throw them into bare ground outside. When rain comes, the clay breaks down and the seeds sprout into flowers that feed bees and butterflies.

5903d2d8c54ddd51.text: Then Follow a flyer. This is a meditation in patience. Some kids will want to catch things. Redirect: "We're following, not catching."

59cda5c407bad0b2.text: What it is for. Find out what happens to all the fallen leaves: they are eaten, and they become the soil the next plants grow in. The skill is looking and touching.

5a4c21cafb05eef8.text: Why it matters. Where does a fallen leaf go is one of the first genuinely big questions a child can investigate to the end.

5a72b0145c9edb32.text: Then Design. A quick sketch with labels is the whole task. The design is the plan they check the finished feeder against in the circle.

5a98a1c2cfb60e7c.text: Counting life. What's living in our grounds?

5b5a15f1d6d3fdd5.text: Why it matters. Every plant in the grounds got there somehow, and watching a seed spin, float or drop from a child's own hand is how seeds travelling stops being a fact and becomes something they saw.

5bb757379c018494.text: Then Act. Throw one seed bomb in the school grounds, the other to take home to throw in a local area. Every bomb is a future patch of wildflowers for insects.

5bdcccfe30fe4c9b.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Have clay and wildflower seeds ready. Find a spot on the school grounds where seed bombs can be thrown.

5d26a6c7226d0a3b.text: How it runs. You start with Count. Set the boundary first: ten steps from where you stand, no further. Pairs work well.

5d314061eba239e4.text: Then Explore and discuss. When a plant is mature it makes seeds. A dandelion is the easy one to show. Wind, rolling, a bird or an animal, or in animal poo. All of those are right.

5d4b70bf485bbcad.text: How it runs. You start with Feel the sun. Face, arms, top of head. Let them notice the warmth: which side is lit, which is in shadow.

5daed321406606ea.text: The idea to carry. On a warm day, some places stay cool: under a tree, against a shaded wall, in long grass, near water.

5e32877c8c517d28.text: What it is for. Autumn is when things get buried for later. Children find seeds, nuts, and berries being stored and reflect on the idea of resting before growing. The skill is touching and looking.

5e43e2ead9792fb9.text: What it is for. Making bird feeders and encouraging wildlife in your school grounds. The skill is looking, listening and touching.

5eb5184ac7c85e57.text: And finish in Circle. Compare the last warm spots. Anticipation of winter. Not fear: curiosity. Close autumn with hope, not loss.

5f09b743370de715.text: Then Touch what's waking. Encourage them to feel temperature differences: warm bark vs cool soil. Notice moisture.

5fa6b5643b21c6c7.text: Then Make. Spend about 15 minutes. Using clay, each child makes 2 seed bombs. Flatten a small piece of clay, press wildflower seeds into it, roll into a ball. One to throw at school, one to take home.

60302486b677d02d.text: The idea to carry. Under every patch of grass is a whole living world: roots, worms, insects, fungi, and soil that is packed with life. Children kneel, dig gently with their fingers, smell the earth, and discover that the ground is not empty at all.

605a79bf091590c5.text: Autumn detectives. How do we know autumn has arrived?

6070181c23465262.text: What it is for. This session is about spreading wildflowers for pollinating insects. The skill is touching and looking.

60a3af8442f01f2a.text: The idea to carry. The pack's turning point. Children hold a fresh leaf and a skeleton leaf, ask what happens between the two, and go hunting for the answer: the decomposers, worms, woodlice, beetles and fungi that break dead material down.

60c64101f9a976ee.text: And finish with The warm colour hunt.

61043f88aca8b1c3.text: How it runs. You start with Notice the smells. Cut grass, warm soil, flowers, rain, hot tarmac. Summer has the strongest smells.

612dcfcce7a1d882.text: How it runs. You start with Notice what's different. Things grew, things died, things moved. The land didn't wait for us. Give them 2 minutes to wander and notice.

6222a88ddfaf6e33.text: Then Introduce. Outside, we will search for seeds and test how they travel from the plant.

62f4cf91ba9b55e1.text: Why it matters. Eating something you harvested and prepared yourself is one of childhood's durable memories, and it quietly carries the pack's biggest idea: the same garden that feeds the worms feeds us, and nothing is wasted.

6303cbb724c78ffa.text: The idea to carry. This is the closing practice of autumn. Winter is coming, and the warmth is retreating: fewer warm days, cooler ground, less sun.

6317e63aec9eeb9e.text: The idea to carry. Every drop of water is a traveller. It falls as rain, soaks into the ground, feeds roots, runs to rivers and the sea, rises into clouds, and falls again.

634ae0264d9657fa.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Bring the bug pots, the magnifying glasses and hand wipes for afterwards. Find your leaf pile the day before: a corner where leaves gather, a hedge bottom, a log. Check it for anything sharp.

635fa926a9562093.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best near flowering plants. Any colourful garden, wildflower patch, or even weeds in cracks will work.

63f81e2caf23fb85.text: Then Wonder. Gentle metaphor. Flowers and children both want to be noticed. Light touch.

64a0adee4958f992.text: Before you go out. Two things to gather. Bring the bug pots or viewers and magnifying glasses. If you can, check your patch the day before: lift a log, see who is home.

64d05c0807b240ec.text: How it runs. You start with Settle. Warm hands notice more. If it's a cold day, a quick round of hand-rubbing at the door doubles as the settle.

65a79e07ba21b51b.text: Promise. Can you find the first sign of spring?

65d57d2eaf3b2af7.text: Before you go out. Five things to gather. Half-fill the jugs before the session and set the trays out: a potion lab with dry tables at the start keeps the mixing as the event. Know your space's plants; the collecting rule is fallen material only, nothing picked, nothing from bins.

665d85ce4002e621.text: And finish in Circle. Puddles, leaves, bark, soil. Follow the journey: ground, roots, river, sea, cloud. Connects to ecology and care.

666bb450a4768b72.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Find an area with accessible soil. A garden bed or base of a tree works well.

6683e21c9ddc4d31.text: Then Wonder. Smell triggers memory more than any other sense. Let them share if they want to.

668b1d4129e0b0b9.text: Then Create. Keep the animal photos on display. Make suggestions, then give them time to be creative.

6717a70d4172b480.text: What it is for. Harvest or handle seasonal food, prepare a simple dish together, and trace where the scraps go next. The skill is making and sharing.

67a324dec6b50864.text: What it is for. Somewhere nearby, creatures are sleeping through winter. Children look for likely hiding spots (under logs, in leaf piles, in wall cracks) without disturbing the sleepers. The skill is looking and touching.

68924df342e72aeb.text: What it is for. Make predictions and test them by mixing natural materials with water, using scientific words for what happens. The skill is predicting and checking.

6898ba1472fab515.text: Then The sharing. Let the fair-sharing problem be genuinely theirs to solve, counting included. Eat together, unhurried; this is the session's celebration and it needs no dressing up.

68b9fe05a1c83b92.text: Then Imagine. Sit with the question. Let the silence do some of the teaching.

68ea8d5fec105c9d.text: Food. What has already been eaten here?

697cc71166d0edac.text: Then Discuss. Discuss why it is important to conserve and help wildlife in the local area. Bird boxes, water dishes, planting berry bushes, leaving seed heads on plants over winter.

69d7d7b680cc6bba.text: What it is for. Understand why trees matter for our existence (humans) and for the other creatures on our planet. The skill is looking and touching.

6a5364867732e143.text: Then Meet the trees. Model the slow flat-hand touch yourself before the children scatter. Name the trees casually as hands land on them. Watch for the child who won't touch: offer the back-of-one-finger version, it counts just the same.

6ab262c7615203f2.text: Why it matters. The warmth children feel outside is the same energy that grows every plant and feeds every food chain. Starting summer by noticing it turns a hot day from something to complain about into something to be grateful for.

6b509f7c28203fc6.text: Then Present. Ask if anyone wants to show their art to the rest of the class.

6badb3ce47345901.text: Then Explore. Class explores green space noticing colours, shapes and patterns while collecting petals, leaves and grass. Remind them: only collect what has already fallen or can be picked without harming the plant.

6bbb69cf6246e629.text: Then Why. The green is the tree's food-maker and it is expensive. Before winter the tree takes it back inside and stores it. The yellows and oranges were in the leaf the whole time, hidden underneath.

6bfa50c9922ccfab.text: The idea to carry. Winter is coming and the garden's animals have no houses, no shops and no coats. Children start by planning their own imaginary winter outside, which surfaces the real list: food, water, shelter, warmth, safety.

6c303535ceabf00d.text: And finish in Circle time. If rubbings are damp, they flatten nicely under a book overnight.

6c7981c3b5abc2e1.text: Abundance. How many living things are within arm's reach?

6c8c3d306a85ea79.text: And finish in Circle. Let a few children hold theirs up for the whole circle. Back into the tree, kept until spring. Say it plainly. It is a good, true answer. No right answer. Ice, wind, weight, the dark. Big guesses welcome.

6cc06ad24612a6d9.text: Then Create. Show the animal photos. Then give them time to be creative.

6d0daf72433765c5.text: Why it matters. Touch is a direct, honest way for a young child to get to know a tree, and it often reaches children who hang back from looking or naming.

6d9b4b1ca1ff9f16.text: What it is for. Autumn is the season of letting go. Children find things that are falling (leaves, seeds, petals) and hold the moment of release. A practice about endings and transformation. The skill is looking and touching.

6dad613997874676.text: Why it matters. Young children often feel the world pauses when they leave it. Coming back to a familiar space and finding it changed teaches something quietly big: nature has its own life and its own clock.

6f9d354ba0493411.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Works best on or just after a rainy day. If dry, look for any standing water, damp surfaces, or dew.

6fc27b67b66f5d20.text: What it is for. Leaves are gone and the hidden structure of trees is revealed. Children see nests, branches, and sky that were invisible in summer. A practice about what becomes visible when things are stripped away. The skill is noticing by looking.

6fc9799bbfa7806f.text: And finish in Circle. Seeds, nuts, berries: nature's savings account. Preparation, survival, planning ahead. Knowledge, friendships, memories. Metaphor territory.

6ff50cf9b2723a47.text: What it is for. Find the fruits and seeds our grounds are giving away this month, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling. The skill is looking and touching.

70003f8abc1e5194.text: Seeds. What could one small seed become?

708ffc0956abc8de.text: And finish in Circle. Let children share. Even pigeons count. Every bird is local wildlife. Worms, seeds, insects, berries. Connects exploration to the feeder-making. Forward-looking. Bird boxes, water, planting, leaving wild corners. After, for you: Your school grounds just got friendlier for birds.

70ba99f8ff4501e1.text: Then Measure a print. Detective work. Reading the ground like a book. Direction, speed, weight.

7196f38383154ba1.text: What it is for. Look closely at minibeasts and discover that all creatures have special roles to help our planet stay alive. The skill is looking and touching.

71b26afb5f688bca.text: Why it matters. The Earth is tilted as it travels round the sun, and in summer our half of the world leans towards it, giving long days and short nights.

720a98702121010c.text: Then Investigate. Urge them to take a closer look: under the leaves, in the soil, along the edge of a log. Lift a leaf like a lid and lower it back the same way.

723685403b8134d8.text: Then Glue. Give the class ideas, drawing on what they saw in nature.

72fe476db5f0d7c2.text: Why it matters. Wind and decay are abstractions to a five year old until a ribbon snaps sideways or a trowel turns up a worm. Giving each force a hands-on moment turns the season's machinery into something a child has personally touched.

734eb279aa0f77ce.text: How it runs. You start with Settle. Gather at the door or the edge of your outdoor space, voices low. Take the slow breath yourself, visibly. The settle sets the register for the whole session.

741fff342f2d550a.text: A5 leaf collage. Create art with nature.

74dc2a9c119f44d2.text: And finish with The winter plans.

757e06208131eb43.text: Then Thank the ground. Pat the earth gently. Walk back.

75d58925e4708e1b.text: The idea to carry. In autumn, deciduous trees let their leaves go, and the ground fills with them. This session sends the class out to meet those leaves and the trees they came from.

770d131717dca2ec.text: The pollinators. Follow one flyer and watch it work.

77214015116212c4.text: The idea to carry. The garden becomes a laboratory. Children collect safe fallen materials, and before anything touches water, they predict: float or sink? Will the water change colour? Then they mix, stir, observe and report what actually happened.

77d6ea24ebe85da1.text: The idea to carry. Winter mud and soft ground hold onto footprints. Birds, dogs, foxes and other animals leave tracks as they pass, and later a child can find them and work out who was here and which way they went.

7814b708e9e70b7e.text: Then Walk the evidence. The compost is the star witness: weeks on, the class's own eyes can confirm the leaves are becoming something else. Read a September journal page aloud beside the November reality. If you kept the winter predictions from session one, produce them here.

7866dfe5caf754c0.text: And finish in Circle. Let 3-4 students share. Encourage specific answers: bird songs, wind, dripping. Optional deeper question.

78b31e1ed1713275.text: And finish in Circle. Let them tell the story of their pollinator's journey. Count if they can. The number often surprises them. Connects to food systems. Powerful for older KS2.

78b7fb381b59a288.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Bring bowls (one per pair or small group), wooden sticks or spoons for crushing, and paper. Find a green space where children can collect fallen petals, leaves, and grass.

7a31af9cb51d45a1.text: The idea to carry. Winter days are short and the light is low, so shadows are long and there are plenty of dim, damp corners. In those shady spots the air is cooler and stiller, and shade-loving plants like moss and ferns do well there.

7a6c3a2641aa35e1.text: From leaf to soil. Where does a fallen leaf go?

7ad5e84c50cf4383.text: The idea to carry. Children collect a variety of leaves outside to create an animal mask they can wear, then show it and tell a story about their chosen animal.

7add3a2a7f595bbb.text: Then The detective brief. Resist naming autumn yourself. The word should arrive from a child, or wait. The mystery frame only works while the answer is theirs to find.

7bd6f3047daeb698.text: What it is for. Explore the different textures and patterns of tree bark using a simple rubbing technique. The skill is noticing by touch.

7d24c41c33b2802f.text: And finish in Circle. Share findings. Decomposition, soil, new life. The cycle. Optional. For reflective classes only.

7d658bb37c1cc5fa.text: Then Talk. Robin, blackbird, pigeon, gull, crow, blue tit, sparrow. Every answer goes on the list, and a made-up bird gets a kind no. Some fly away to warmer places. Some stay, and spend the whole short day looking for food.

7d722cefca58df94.text: Then Sort. Back inside, hand out the animal picture cards in small groups. Go through the correct answers as a class. Hedgehog, dormouse, bat: hibernate. Swallow, house martin: migrate. Robin, blackbird, squirrel: adapt.

7d9eb0808e993f9f.text: Why it matters. Water is everywhere and easy to ignore. Following its journey gives children a first, wonder-filled grasp of the water cycle and of how everything in nature is connected and reused.

7dc98790489c0d50.text: Why it matters. This is the last winter session and its emotional peak. After weeks of cold, finding the first sign of spring gives children a real feeling of hope and of a cycle turning.

7e1e7285166dfd9d.text: What it is for. Meet and name leaves from common trees, and notice how they differ. The skill is naming and noticing.

7e750048a28d8fbd.text: Then Hang. Discuss good spots as a group before anyone hangs anything. A branch at adult height, a fence hook, the feeder pole if there is one.

7eca45af60be4ae6.text: What it is for. Discover that dead leaves are broken down by living things, and build a class compost to watch it happen. The skill is watching change over time.

7eee6ebb206e9ab1.text: Then Wonder. Kids love this idea. Some will say "amazing." Acknowledge that rest is essential, for animals and for us.

7fb2813966e8ec90.text: Why it matters. Shade is easy to take for granted until a hot day. Noticing that a living tree creates shelter, and that soil and stone hold coolness, helps children see the outdoors as something that looks after them.

7fce0ecbf4a2f6f0.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. First session back after summer. Walk the grounds yourself first if possible, notice what changed.

803db2cc27549fbb.text: Then The potion lab. Feed the vocabulary while it has something to grip: predict, observe, compare, float, sink, change, texture. Words land when the thing they name is in front of the child. The wet leaf against the dry leaf is texture change made touchable.

8052738bbf421dbc.text: What it is for. Children find and hold seeds: dandelion fluff, acorns, berries, grass seeds. Each one contains a whole future. A practice about potential and careful attention. The skill is touching and looking.

80cbf26ff4b22a94.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best near flowering plants on a warm day when insects are active. Scout for bee-friendly areas.

8135ab70fe1fe537.text: Then Wonder. Pollination without the textbook. They're witnessing it happen.

8174367456b4b750.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a sunny day. Note which direction is west (sunset) before going out.

81e6605ff9a1bdbb.text: Then Follow the wind. The wind is invisible but you can see its effects everywhere. Track what it touches.

823187d31af79319.text: Winter survival sort. How do animals survive the cold?

827cd165cc06e54c.text: Then Thank the sun. 93 million miles. You can mention that if you want. Kids love the number.

82a65c1a3192ca07.text: The idea to carry. In early spring the land begins to stir. Buds swell, green shoots push up, birds sing more, and the soil softens as it warms.

82ace642e7b68bac.text: And finish in Circle time. Combine everyone's totals on the board into one big class tally chart. Conkers and acorns fall straight down and roll, so they gather under their own tree. That is why one tree gives so many.

83508c57e708e6d2.text: Then Put it back. Place it gently. Don't throw. Walk back.

8431ba0944c2c533.text: How it runs. You start with Find a sign. A swelling bud, a snowdrop, longer daylight, a bird singing more loudly. The first whispers of change.

8522e5ecf43189af.text: And finish in Circle. Let students describe what they saw. Twigs, mud, silk, leaves. Open-ended, connects to their own lives.

85adc70cb81a1ec7.text: The idea to carry. Seeds on plants and how they come to be there. Indoors first: what is a seed, and have you ever found one.

85b3d9aa630c1b4f.text: Then Take outside. Leaves from the ground only. The oldest ones are under the fresh ones, and under hedges and along walls. Lift a leaf like a lid and lower it back the same way. Look, do not lift the creatures.

8610dc70985ae898.text: Tree bark rubbings. Every tree wears its own coat.

864d37f6112e1424.text: What it is for. Notice that the light is going and the year is turning, and find the four answers the living things around us give to winter: store it, sleep through it, leave, or die back and wait underground. The skill is looking and wondering.

86fe1e49701dd551.text: The idea to carry. One session, three hats. The science hat: collect fallen leaves and sort them by colour, shape and size. The maker hat: turn the sorted leaves into an animal mask.

872031f739e423fb.text: Then Introduce. Food, water, shelter. Short days and frozen ground make food the hardest. Show a picture of a simple bottle bird feeder. We do not need to be expert builders.

88db3ff6a8f4a08e.text: The idea to carry. This is the closing practice of spring. Children walk slowly, choose three living things they want to thank, stand with each one, and say its name and thank you, out loud.

89ab63c5c3b181ef.text: Then Wonder. This is the hardest step. Silence is fine. Some kids will say happy or weird or nothing. All good. You might share what you feel first to give permission.

8a27fd3550b017a4.text: The idea to carry. Children identify and observe plants in their local environment, explore how plants produce seeds, and investigate how seeds travel to new places.

8aacc346b2b1068a.text: Hibernation. Where might something be sleeping all winter?

8ab654e586c7ca7b.text: Then Catch one. A fallen leaf was connected to a tree for months. Now it's free. Feel the weight of that lightness.

8b23f2e37afd14ba.text: What it is for. A patient observation practice. Children find a flying insect (a bee, butterfly, or hoverfly) and follow it slowly, watching it work from flower to flower. The skill is looking and listening.

8c34b19c5976370a.text: Then Show and tell. Help each child build a sentence like that one: I am, I live, I come out. Give each child their turn. A shy one can say just the first line.

8cc86f7f24904c1d.text: What it is for. The autumn colour change in real time. Children find leaves halfway between green and gold, catalogue the arriving and departing colours, and witness transformation happening slowly. The skill is noticing by looking.

8d212148279bcadb.text: The idea to carry. Autumn is when nature banks for the future. Trees drop seeds, nuts and berries, squirrels bury acorns, seeds work their way into cracks in the ground, and bulbs sit waiting underground.

8ea5d14de46b82cb.text: Then Sort and measure. Chalk two circles on the ground, or lay out two hoops, if sorting on the ground helps.

8f0596e8ed67b4ff.text: Before you go out. Six things to gather. Print the mask template, one per child. Have a few photos of common animals ready to show.

8f6133d1a8f1b087.text: Then Look. Three places to look, in this order: the hedge and low branches, the ground under them, then the sky. Binoculars go to whoever has found something, not whoever asks.

8f87350324f4a281.text: Then Thank the rain. Simple. Walk back.

8fdcba4d7bd833d9.text: How it runs. You start with Talk. Discussion about wildflowers and how they spread: wind carries seeds, animals carry them on fur or in droppings, water moves them, people plant them. Some arrived by accident. Some have been here longer than the school.

90030d22f3382a6b.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Peel the crayons the day before. Take one rubbing yourself to show at the start, and pick out four or five trees with different bark within a short walk.

903260128643550e.text: Then Hold the warmth. Present-moment awareness. The warmth of autumn is finite and precious.

90625a3842f43cd5.text: Why it matters. Autumn is the one month of the year when a whole plant's plan is lying on the ground where a five-year-old can pick it up.

907d6b392d6066b6.text: The idea to carry. In autumn, deciduous trees stop making the green that fills their leaves all summer. As the green fades, the yellows, oranges, reds and browns that were hidden underneath begin to show.

91359945d6edfe2d.text: Five words to have ready. Each has a plain definition and a child's version, already written.

91589e96c74315e9.text: Breath. Can you see your own breath?

917ef2b1b987b241.text: Meet your tree. Choosing a tree to visit all year.

93361fd1d49b9492.text: The idea to carry. What happens to a leaf after it falls. Indoors first, children say what tells them it is autumn, then meet the word decompose: after a leaf falls it slowly breaks down, with help from friendly garden creatures.

9382174cd831fa1c.text: And finish in Circle. Compare observations. Everyone sees different things. Imagination + ecology. Personal connection.

9396be2ca7e3071c.text: Soil. What is the ground made of?

94c11e044c9b3133.text: The idea to carry. Children gather the fruits and seeds their grounds are letting go this month, look closely at what each one is wearing, drop them to see how they travel, and work out what every seed carries: a plant, a packed lunch, a coat, and a way of travelling.

94c68674d3dfe372.text: How it runs. You start with Find a hiding spot. Under logs, in leaf piles, in cracks in walls, under stones. Don't disturb. Just look for likely spots.

94ea811b5a692c67.text: Then Water: following the rain. If the week has been dry, pour your jar of water slowly onto a patch of soil and watch it together: where does it go? The question is honest either way, and disappearing-into-the-ground is the answer that links water to roots.

95485c221d87b8c3.text: How it runs. You start with Find what was hidden. Nests, branches, the shape of trunks, buildings behind trees, the sky itself. Winter reveals.

95cbc33a94e61a5e.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in areas where nuts, seeds, or berries can be found on the ground.

973e64d94eb3d7ff.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation. Every outdoor space has food chains happening.

97c440b900d1c60f.text: What it is for. Make an animal mask from leaves and begin to tell a story about your chosen animal. The skill is telling a story.

97d797b603f8400c.text: And finish in Circle. Go around the circle. Every answer is valid. Often the gratitude that surprises us is the most real. Close the season with this. Let them sit with the feeling.

97d8dafdf8bcd91e.text: How it runs. You start with Walk. One leaf each, from the ground, chosen for its colour. Ask them not to pull leaves off a branch: those have not finished yet.

987e6a6f6913eadb.text: Then Find your breath. Body temperature is remarkable. We generate heat constantly. In winter you can feel the contrast.

989785010900e942.text: Why it matters. This is where noticing becomes caring. A child who has built a leaf pile for hedgehogs or beetles has crossed from watching nature to helping it, and an untidy corner defended for the animals' sake reframes what a good garden even is.

98995cf8338a735c.text: Quiet. What is the quietest sound you can hear?

994f3c534abf734f.text: What it is for. A return to the ground. Children pick up handfuls of soil, smell it, squeeze it, and discover that everything that ever lived here is now part of the earth beneath their feet. The skill is touching and smelling.

9988caa115b28f71.text: What it is for. A perception exercise. Children discover that green is not one colour but dozens: dark moss, bright leaf, pale lichen, emerald grass. Then they name their favourite with a feeling-word. The skill is looking.

9a14787cd051ae3b.text: Bark rubbings. Every tree wears its own coat.

9aba07db297b1fcc.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a cold day when breath is visible. The colder, the better for this practice.

9abdaa6c96f7c842.text: Then Find who eats. Holes in leaves, nibbled edges, pecked fruit, hollowed-out acorns. Evidence of feeding.

9ada509b6e9a3ac7.text: Then Wonder. It could be beauty, shade, oxygen, food, sound. Personal reasons.

9c076b5899e81e00.text: Then Watch them work. Sit still for 2 minutes and just observe. Movement is the clue.

9c4ccffb03009740.text: Why it matters. Prediction is the move that turns play into science. A child who says out loud what they expect, and then watches, has run a real experiment, and being cheerfully wrong teaches the most valuable lesson in the room: looking beats guessing.

9c82d860c069a96c.text: What it is for. Design and build a simple bird feeder using a recycled plastic bottle. The skill is designing and making.

9ce5627878da634a.text: Then Look closer. Looking at different flowers in more depth. Where are their seeds? How might they be gathered? Notice wildflower seedlings growing near parent plants. Some seeds are in pods, some in heads, some hidden inside.

9d5b650b1ab8d208.text: Then Feel the shelter. Hibernation spots are chosen carefully. Feel why this spot works: blocked from wind, insulated by leaves.

9d6b157802eaf56b.text: Why it matters. Learning to be still and really listen is a skill children rarely get to practise, and autumn gives the perfect conditions: a quieter world where subtle sounds can finally be heard.

9d9847adb9ac1d62.text: Why it matters. A named, chosen tree gives a class a single living thing to return to across the whole year, and returning is where real nature connection grows.

9d9b753f6b5eda66.text: Then Create and glue. Set up before you call the children over: one A5 card each, glue sticks along the table, all the collected leaves pooled in the middle so every child chooses from the shared gathering.

9dc3f33ef2a8ad2b.text: Then Listen. Take the class to a spot with a good view of trees, sky, or the feeder if there is one. Do the minute yourself, visibly. The quiet lasts longer if you are in it too.

9dfda80eacf574a8.text: Then Make. Using collected nature, crush in bowls and use as painting medium with their hands. Different plants give different colours: grass gives green, petals give pinks/yellows/purples, soil gives brown. Let them experiment and mix.

9e1d1285a6b28748.text: Why leaves turn. Where does the green go?

9eeec8c269099014.text: Then Welcome it back. A greeting after absence. Walk back together.

9fcebd0b36a4c361.text: Then Wonder. Patience and presence. Autumn teaches slowness.

a0bf8047552e6b11.text: Then Collect. Ground-only collecting keeps the trees whole and keeps this session repeatable all autumn. Name the trees casually as you walk: oak, maple, birch. Children absorb a name fastest when they hear it beside the real leaf.

a1f8637501a37f7d.text: Then The winter shopping trip. If the masks from session two survived, this is their encore: children can shop as their own creature. Berries stay on the bush, looking only; the food hunt is a stocktake, not a harvest.

a228b67c060a9769.text: Then Introduce. Food, warmth, shelter. Write the answers on the board. Three words on the board, one example under each. The cards will be sorted under these later.

a2a90cbdd4e333d0.text: And finish in Circle. Compare numbers. Usually way more than expected. Share the creative names. Celebrate imagination. Connects to biodiversity, light, seasons.

a2e7776a667852bc.text: And finish in Circle. Let children share their discoveries. Which plants gave the strongest colour? Often the colours are not what children expect. Green leaves can give yellow. Red petals can give pink. Connects making to feeling. The medium IS the message.

a2f7515161c8860b.text: How it runs. You start with Wonder. Ask it before you go out and let it sit. Most children have never noticed the absence.

a300e0a153950948.text: Then The evidence hunt. Steer the wander past the three changes you scouted, without pointing. Kneel beside whoever finds one and ask what they think happened here. The question does more than the answer.

a30ec14fb639eb50.text: Before you go out. Five things to gather. Choose the compost's spot in advance: on soil if possible, reachable in wet shoes, visible enough that visiting it stays easy. Save fruit and vegetable scraps from snack for a few days beforehand. Nothing cooked, no meat, no dairy.

a3de426f5f112302.text: Why it matters. The idea that something can look finished, a fallen acorn, a dropped berry, yet hold a whole new plant or a whole next spring inside it, is a quietly powerful one for young children.

a3e9021aff755689.text: Making bird feeders. What do birds find hard to find in winter, and how could we help?

a4010fb950bc2a0a.text: Then Wonder. The tree didn't mean to shelter you, but it does. That's a gift.

a40537731a3a0f72.text: And finish in Circle. Hedge, ground, sky. Notice together that different birds were in different places. Food. A short day, a cold night, and a small body to keep warm. This is the question the bird feeders lesson answers with our hands.

a416ccf9cdc7ff36.text: Then Wonder. Gratitude for being warm-blooded. For being alive. For the body doing its job without being asked.

a4e6c66e607b5d35.text: The idea to carry. What happens to a leaf after it falls. Children start by saying what tells them it is autumn, then meet the word decompose: after a leaf falls it slowly breaks down, with help from friendly garden creatures.

a5bddb0402102607.text: Then Creatures. e.g. birds for homes and food (nuts and fruit), insects.

a606e4345a2c045b.text: Then Send it on. The leaf will become soil. That's not an ending. Walk back.

a6a00ca2e6b26014.text: How it runs. You start with Find a builder. Birds with nests, insects with webs, squirrels with dens. Any creature making shelter.

a7dbfad0f1e34d4d.text: And finish with Open the compost diary. The diary is the pack's long game: five minutes at the heap each week, one line or drawing per visit. What has changed, what has disappeared, who is visiting. Date every entry.

a823b31b8ebcfbd9.text: Bird feeders. Making bird feeders and encouraging wildlife in your school grounds.

a8abd532c065025a.text: And finish in Circle. Puddles, leaves, grass, metal surfaces. It goes back to being water. Nothing is permanent. Optional. Transformation theme.

a922e927b2da34db.text: Fruit and seed. What is your seed wearing, and what is it for?

a97badec5805fc6b.text: The idea to carry. For the last practice of summer, children take ten steps, stop, and meet every living thing within arm's reach: grass blades, ants, moss, a beetle, a bird overhead, a crusty patch of lichen on a wall.

a9d9a365e0c3b85c.text: The idea to carry. On a cold day you can see your own breath. The warm, damp air from inside your body meets the cold air outside and turns to a little cloud of mist, just for a moment.

a9eb45c7961976dc.text: Then Living. Four signs they can test anything against. Try them on a bird, a tree, a stone.

aa2220a9baaa5e77.text: Long day. Where will the sun set tonight?

aa612cfa50d5632c.text: And finish in Circle. Encourage specific, descriptive language. Smell-memory connection. Often surprising stories emerge. Connects seasons, anticipation.

aa91ecbbf166d8d6.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather.

aac7e65acc90ba7d.text: And finish with Circle and feedback. Each child gets a turn. A shy one can say just the first line. If thirty turns will not fit, pairs first, then five volunteers. Keep the masks. They can come out again whenever an animal turns up in a lesson.

abb94037ce5f8d9c.text: And finish in Circle. Connects school space to home space. Personal connection to the season. Sets up autumn. Anticipation.

abdc787d9ee00d99.text: Then Hear. Try thirty seconds of complete silence first. The longer the quiet, the more they hear.

ac13659587ae373c.text: What it is for. Investigate how soil, wind and water are each changing the garden, and find autumn's warm colours. The skill is investigating.

ad24984b373c7b6e.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best after rain or frost when the ground is soft or marked. Muddy areas show tracks best.

ae4a5991e452627d.text: What it is for. The first practice of spring. Children look and listen for signs that the land is waking from winter: new shoots, returning birds, softening soil. The skill is looking and listening.

af9bca6e65219062.text: Getting ready for winter. Who is getting ready for the cold?

b02158cb27bda6c5.text: Then Experiment. Let the drops repeat. Swap roles so both children hold and both children watch.

b03ca41c1c80a041.text: And finish in Circle. Let 3-4 students share. No right answers. Encourage sensory words: soft, sticky, cool, delicate. Optional. Only for classes ready for deeper reflection.

b03feca24026511f.text: Then Sort. The colour line is a timeline. Green fell this week, brown fell long ago.

b19ab2bd06f4bb97.text: The idea to carry. Autumn is the season of letting go. Deciduous trees stop feeding their leaves, the leaves change colour and loosen, and one by one they fall.

b299a880e8c3c103.text: Then Take outside. Give each pair a pot. Point them toward trees, shrubs and flowerbeds to search. Keep it simple: when a plant is mature it makes seeds. A dandelion is the easy one to show.

b2ba28ad65a0c827.text: The idea to carry. Seeds on plants and how they come to be there. Children search the grounds for plants, find where the seeds are, and work out how seeds arrive in a place.

b31cfb0ee77ae304.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best in the morning when birds are most active feeding. Near feeders if your school has them.

b3d7dafc0bd50050.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a mild day when insects and birds are active. Near trees or hedges is ideal.

b3e50ba6ba168f1e.text: What it is for. Create art with nature, taking influence from what the children see around them. The skill is touching and looking.

b4ca6bcbfe888a22.text: And finish in Circle. Describe shape, size, direction. Deduction. Match prints to animals. Perspective-taking. Empathy practice.

b4d46fa2db241835.text: Then Wonder. Subtle sounds emerge in silence. Your own breathing. A faraway bird. Water somewhere.

b4e4d5e243aafd5e.text: Then Build the class compost. Balance and air are the two adult jobs: roughly more brown than green, and no squashing the heap flat. Nothing cooked, no meat, no dairy, ever. Everyone should get at least one handful into the heap; the compost has to be theirs.

b60832dbdc9a769f.text: What it is for. In cold air, you can see your own breath, visible proof of being alive. Children watch their warmth meet the cold and discover that their body is a furnace. The skill is noticing by looking.

b6ed7a22f9a76a62.text: The idea to carry. The closing session builds one thing: the connection.

b705b30d54291ad7.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. No preparation needed. Works in any outdoor space.

b75444c047282a29.text: And finish in Circle time. Add the sheets up on the board, one tick per kind of bird. Food. A short day, a cold night, and a small body to keep warm. This is the question the bird feeders lesson answers with our hands.

b7f8957afb335b4f.text: Then Explore. Explore natural food for birds in your green space: worms in the soil, seeds on plants, insects on leaves, berries on bushes. What is already here for them? Is there enough?

b850a82bd96f1bd7.text: And finish in Circle. Build food chains together verbally. Extend the chain. Kids love this. Trace it back to sun, soil, water.

b88de83fbb1ca773.text: What it is for. Notice everything that is alive around you and begin to work out what it means to be living - breathing, growing, reproducing, dying. The skill is looking and listening.

b8cac17b3bacefa0.text: Wind. Where do you feel the wind, and what does it move?

b9a2b2f04d1c0179.text: Why it matters. Some children are uneasy about darkness. This session meets that gently and reframes the dark as a place where quiet things thrive, not a place to fear.

ba1c1e07a9eb29dd.text: Then Meet. Bring the class back together. Woodlice, worms, millipedes, slugs, springtails, and the white threads running through the wet leaves: all of them are eating.

ba6b7ac8ca446b2a.text: And finish in Circle. Simple observation. Joy in visibility. Science connection: metabolism, food as fuel, blood circulation. Generosity metaphor.
