ba96af60fe04834c.text: Shade. Where is the coolest place, and what made it?

ba9d09dec0f16758.text: Then Four answers. Four answers they can hold anything against. Try them on a squirrel, a hedgehog, a swallow, a daffodil.

bbd2174a23cd22f6.text: What it is for. The final summer practice. Children count everything alive within arm's reach and discover they are standing in a crowd of living things. A practice about noticing how much life surrounds us. The skill is noticing by looking.

bc3567c8a89e6b41.text: Then Build the winter homes. Say the strange truth out loud: we usually tidy the garden, and today we are untidying it on purpose, because a too-tidy garden has nowhere to sleep. The hands-off rule after building matters; a checked-daily leaf pile is a disturbed one.

bc99ab736b1d373a.text: Then Wonder. A philosophical moment. Don't explain. Just let them sit with it.

be914a1bbb947e0d.text: Why it matters. Food chains are usually taught from a book. Here children read them off the real world, from marks left in real leaves.

bea8e9acab3a9772.text: What it is for. The closing practice of spring. Children walk slowly, choose three living things, and thank them by name. A practice in gratitude, attention, and speaking kindness aloud. The skill is feeling and looking.

bfa6f46fac4fd327.text: Then Crumble. This is the moment of the lesson. Dig down to where the leaves have stopped looking like leaves. Rub it between finger and thumb: dark, damp, crumbly, and it used to be a tree.

bff8eb9e72a695ea.text: Then Thank them all. Close the summer season. A collective thank you. Walk back together slowly.

c0a42bc3d4c64417.text: What it is for. Observe seasonal changes in plants, and explore what happens to fallen leaves as they decompose and how nutrients are returned to the soil. The skill is looking closely.

c153f756c88ae326.text: Then Leave it be. Anti-extraction principle. We observe, we don't take. Walk back.

c2336d12a78cd18a.text: Why it matters. Children often think a bare tree is a dead tree. It isn't. It is resting, holding next year's leaves inside tiny buds.

c3b7230cfe54d66c.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Fill a jar with water the day before in case it has not rained: a poured puddle is an honest stand-in for a rained one. Check your digging patch is free of glass and litter.

c3caf4d1796b3751.text: And finish with Name the potion. The naming is the imagination beat and it has done its job in two minutes; hold the last minute for the surprise question, which is the science walking out of the door with them.

c4da4a5c28d4a239.text: Then Explore. Leaves from the ground only. The oldest ones are under the fresh ones, and under hedges and along walls.

c508188cd41fd95e.text: What it is for. Spring is building season. Birds make nests, insects spin webs, creatures find shelter. Children observe the builders at work and imagine their labour. The skill is looking and listening.

c5f728f11c1a4b14.text: What it is for. Meet trees up close by touch, and keep a rubbing of each tree's own pattern. The skill is noticing by touch.

c68da442c02a10b1.text: Then Travel. Hold a sycamore key up high and let it go, then a conker. The class sees the difference before anyone explains it.

c702ea6fe0c27079.text: Then Discuss. Prompt children to discuss amongst themselves. They produce the air we need to breathe (oxygen).

c775b5551976a94b.text: Then Look. Everything on the tray is wearing something: a wing, a cup, a shell, a skin, a hook. The wearing is the whole lesson.

c810faec5ec50d9c.text: And finish in Circle. Close with the promise of return: "We'll visit again and see what our tree has been doing." The friendship is the point; every later session can begin or end with a one-minute hello to the class tree.

c83373d8c347e8d0.text: Conker and acorn maths trail. Which is easier to find, conkers or acorns?

c85cc9c3e0559af4.text: Before you go out. No preparation needed. Works in any green space with some wildflowers or garden flowers.

c877a9498a7cfa86.text: From garden to table. How does the garden feed us?

c93e8dc5ba5863f3.text: How it runs. You start with Find something frozen. If there's no frost, look for cold: the coldest surface, condensation on metal, breath visible in air.

c96ebd3f1ca4419d.text: The idea to carry. Children point to where the sun is now and where it will set, hunt for the longest and shortest shadows, and notice how late the summer light lasts.

c9994b1eae8a65df.text: Then Thank the tree. Vulnerability as strength. Walk back.

ca088b3f142b28c8.text: The idea to carry. Some animals get through winter by sleeping through it. Hedgehogs, frogs, and many insects find a sheltered spot, slow their bodies right down, and stay hidden until spring.

caca921aaed932e5.text: Gratitude walk. Finding three living things to thank.

cb0d88b17849728c.text: The nature potion lab. What happens when we mix materials from nature?

cb74647e402008ca.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Gather the season's physical trail before the session: journals, any kept artwork, the winter predictions you wrote down in session one.

cb8b028e14cb3513.text: The idea to carry. Everything outside is food for something. Leaves feed caterpillars, seeds feed birds, nectar feeds bees, berries feed many creatures at once. Rather than watching the eating happen, children look for the evidence of it: holes in leaves, nibbled edges, pecked fruit.

ccca82d1f14cbd37.text: What it is for. Everything is food for something. Children find evidence of feeding (nibbled leaves, pecked fruit, nectar being collected) and discover their schoolyard is a living food web. The skill is looking and touching.

ccd6abacf661ea05.text: Then Introduce. Show a completed bark rubbing. Explain the technique: hold the paper flat against the trunk and rub the side of a crayon over it, and the pattern underneath comes through.

ccf422f17e133e53.text: Then Hold the promise. An acorn, a conker, a rosehip. Each one contains next spring.

cd374458ebc166c9.text: What it is for. The final winter practice. Children search for the first signs that spring is coming: a swelling bud, a snowdrop, longer daylight. Proof that the cycle continues. The skill is looking and touching.

cdab95d5362811d0.text: Why it matters. Every plant in the grounds got there somehow.

cdcbfbde82b76b0f.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best when leaves are actively falling. Any area with deciduous trees works.

cdf427fcded95d37.text: And finish with The detectives report. Write two or three of their winter predictions somewhere you can keep. Session eight returns to them, and children meeting their own September guesses in December is one of the best moments in the pack.

cead2081628f989f.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Bring oranges (one per pair), birdseed, and string. Have a knife ready to halve the oranges (teacher does this). Find trees where feeders can be hung.

cf20aca65fefe2fe.text: Then Find the turning leaf. A half-turned leaf is autumn captured. Two colours on one surface.

cf5ee4bb3228e5b2.text: Why it matters. Children walk on soil every day without ever really meeting it.

cff6c6a9f19611fe.text: Why it matters. Every child has been told that leaves change colour in autumn; almost none have been told why, and the real reason is simple enough for a five-year-old.

d00169a362d70fd1.text: Then Thank the dark. Balance. Walk back into the light together.

d0bad131bf617859.text: Then Touch the bud. A bud is packed with leaves. A bulb tip pushing through soil. Concentrated potential.

d0c6e3d94385b5b8.text: Then Wonder. Some kids will find it gross. That's a valid feeling too.

d0dc7d34609a494a.text: What it is for. Children explore where the sun is touching: their bodies, surfaces, the ground. A practice about solar energy, warmth as nourishment, and the 93-million-mile journey of light. The skill is touching and looking.

d12c8694a276144a.text: And finish in Circle. We borrow, we look, we give back. The whole lesson in one move. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist.

d12e19c2e92469a9.text: Why it matters. This is art lesson, science lesson, and sensory lesson in one. Children learn where colours come from — a question most adults can't answer. They touch textures they usually walk past. And the art itself celebrates nature rather than extracting from it.

d18d7b71dfce2c00.text: Then Collect. Only leaves that have already fallen. Nothing picked from a living plant. Collect at least thirty. Better too many than not enough.

d1ac5d49669b8840.text: Why it matters. Ending autumn by seeking out its last warmth teaches children to treasure something exactly because it is fleeting, a gentle, hopeful lesson rather than a sad one.

d1d50f2314ad1344.text: Why it matters. Autumn is a countdown a child can watch happening.

d1eb7aa669db9311.text: How it runs. You start with Find water. Even on dry days there's moisture somewhere. Dew, drainage, damp bark.

d2510800bdd4f819.text: Then Predictions first. Collect a few predictions loudly enough that the room hears them: the payoff in the next phase needs the guesses on record. Model being wrong with relish yourself: predict something confidently, be wrong, be delighted.

d263f03f5d2ce4cb.text: Why it matters. The question this session opens with, why is the playground not buried in leaves, has an answer a child can hold in their hand. Nothing here is thrown away: it is eaten, and it becomes the next thing.

d2b017ba2ec6b370.text: Getting ready for winter. How do animals prepare for winter?

d2b05cd77a7d0d86.text: What it is for. An invisible force made visible. Children feel the wind on their skin, watch what it moves, and reflect on something that touches everything but holds nothing. The skill is touching and listening.

d30035c7962d9caf.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best during peak autumn colour (October). Any area with deciduous trees.

d3dab8b705cf9941.text: Then Explore. Give each pair a pot. Point them toward trees, shrubs and flowerbeds to search. When a plant is mature it makes seeds. A dandelion is the easy one to show. Wind, rolling, a bird or an animal, or in animal poo.

d4a3e90f5e11c9f2.text: Where the leaves go. Why is our playground not buried in leaves?

d50b8437160a3fe0.text: Then Wonder. Shared survival. Shared anticipation. This is the emotional peak of the winter season.

d50c14d4b69fc3fa.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Best on a cool autumn day when warmth is noticeable. Scout for sun-warmed surfaces.

d55874fce28a87f1.text: How it runs. You start with Talk. Talk about the different birds you might see locally. Listen for birdsong. Look for movement in trees and hedges. Common ones: robins, blue tits, sparrows, blackbirds, pigeons.

d56f500d36bb60bf.text: Then Hold the soil. Crumbly, damp, gritty, smooth. Each type of soil tells a story about what lives in it.

d58483837f3b9601.text: Why it matters. A five-year-old already knows winter is cold and food is scarce. Three named ways out of that, sleep through it, leave, or change, turn a worry into a way of looking at every animal they meet.

d5864fa1bb12d263.text: Then Choose. Give each candidate tree a real visit: a minute standing under it, hands on bark, faces up.

d5b43081499db9e8.text: Before you go out. Six things to gather. Collect and rinse the bottles a week ahead, one per pair. Have a picture of a simple bottle feeder to show, and cut a test hole in one bottle yourself so you know how the plastic behaves.

d618b950ac46c66b.text: What it is for. Children seek out the coolest spots and discover microclimates: how a tree creates shelter, how soil holds moisture, how shade is a gift from something alive. The skill is touching and listening.

d716705602fdc76b.text: How it runs. You start with Find something opening. Give them 2 minutes to walk and look. Don't direct where. Let them wander. Buds, flowers, even cracks in pavement where green pushes through. Anything opening counts.

d729702885b48764.text: Natural paint making. Using natural resources to create.

d7e028d67bd34126.text: Then The making. Hands washed first, boards out, one job per child to start: washers, tearers, cutters, mixers, and rotate. The dish does not matter; the making does. Keep every scrap and peel in one bowl, visibly: it has a journey to finish later.

d7fb5217562a9214.text: Ice. What does frozen feel like?

d81cc4931afa4794.text: The idea to carry. Many animals leave or hide away in winter, but some birds stay all season. They spend their short cold days working hard to find enough to eat: hopping across grass, searching hedges, pecking at the ground.

d8a71a1c36777559.text: The idea to carry. This session turns getting to know trees into a lasting friendship. The class visits the trees in their grounds, stands under each one, looks up through its branches and touches its coat, then chooses together the tree that will be their own.

d8eaa677d3536cf0.text: Then Sit in the cool. A tree made shade. Soil holds moisture. Stone stays cool. They're discovering microclimates.

d91e532403c19966.text: How it runs. You start with Notice what's missing. Fewer birds singing. Fewer insects buzzing. The soundscape of autumn is quieter than summer.

da13a883b59274a9.text: What it is for. A practice about water: where it comes from, where it goes, and the extraordinary journey every raindrop has taken. Sensory engagement with puddles, drips, and damp surfaces. The skill is listening and touching.

da2698d1f8f7de43.text: The idea to carry. Three short investigations in one session: earth, air and water, each met with hands and senses rather than words.

dacb2eae558fbc2d.text: What it is for. Find out why leaves change colour and fall: the tree is taking its green back in before winter, and the other colours were there all along. The skill is looking closely.

db74b79d2c9aa08f.text: Why it matters. Hibernation gives children a lovely, gentle idea: that rest is not laziness but survival, and that a sleeping creature deserves to be left in peace.

dc018dc06bed5243.text: Why it matters. Soil is easy to walk over and never think about, yet it holds the roots that feed every plant and the creatures that keep it healthy. Getting hands in the earth is grounding, sensory, and a little brave.

dc1dd85941aa8bda.text: Why it matters. Naming what is alive is the first step to caring about it. A child who has counted dozens of living things in one corner of the playground never sees "nothing" there again.

dc70ded4862493f0.text: Then Hunt. Nibbled nuts, empty shells, a hole at the bottom of a hedge, a web, a nest showing now the leaves are thinning, a bush stripped of its berries. Evidence, not animals.

dc9200fd2da5a9ae.text: The idea to carry. Children spend time quietly observing birds around the school grounds and use a simple spotter sheet to identify what they see. Indoors first: which birds might we see, what sounds might we hear, and what a bird watcher does.

dcb02baf3cdedc40.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Find an area with accessible soil (not paved). A garden bed, grassy area, or bare earth patch.

dcf18ad7137cfc79.text: And finish in Circle. The most subtle observation wins. Bees, lawn mowers, birdsong. Where did they go? Personal preference. No right answer.

dd9043da657046a1.text: Then Whisper hello. Model this yourself first. Walk back together in quiet.

ddbf3aa761d16172.text: Then Explore. Explore your green space and notice flowers. Smell, touch, look closely. How many different kinds can they find? What colours? What shapes? Which ones have visitors?

ddff9ef6630640f1.text: And finish in Circle time. Introduce the idea of nature's recycling system: the leaf falls, the creatures break it down, the soil gets the goodness, a new plant grows.

de25269ac4a28c67.text: Then Introduce. Show the photos for inspiration: fox, hedgehog, owl, robin. The mask will be made from things we collect outside.

dee10fd29548cdaa.text: Then Collect. Search for conkers and acorns already on the ground. Nothing picked from the trees.

df1ae909c7e40dc5.text: Then Go close. Encourage them to use fingertips. Notice temperature, texture, moisture. Some kids will want to pick things. Redirect: Can you know it without taking it?

df69e2b721b56488.text: How it runs. You start with Find what's stored away. Squirrels burying nuts, seeds falling into cracks, berries dropping. Nature is banking for the future.

df8e1481dae79827.text: Then Wish it well. Gentle. Respectful of the sleeping creature. Walk back quietly.

dfd9cd45115e21c7.text: Falling. What here is letting go?

e018842c60027b10.text: The idea to carry. Children go outside to investigate the life cycle of a leaf: from when it grows on a tree and falls in autumn, through decomposition, to how its nutrients return to the soil and support new plant growth.

e07f5308456bd95d.text: And finish in Circle. Close by naming what you noticed the children doing: "I saw people turning leaves over to meet both sides." Naming the skill out loud is how it sticks.

e160065a7f67854f.text: Then Take outside. Search for conkers and acorns already on the ground. Nothing picked from the trees. Chalk two circles on the ground, or lay out two hoops, if sorting on the ground helps.

e182b6c8e545caf0.text: Before you go out. Nothing to bring.

e1e07f7c80c04b15.text: Then The mystery of the missing leaves. If the ground offers one, show a leaf skeleton or a half-rotted leaf beside the fresh one: the same object at two points in time. Let the gap between them do the asking.

e2f4fda7959829c6.text: How it runs. You start with Find the coolest spot. Under a tree, against a north-facing wall, near water, in long grass. Let them explore.

e31ec35e502e067e.text: Then Wonder. Seasonal metaphor for inner life. Light touch. Optional for younger groups.

e37413d1b105048d.text: Before you go out. Four things to gather. Print the bird spotter sheet, one per pair. If the school has a feeder or a bird table, check it is stocked the day before: it brings the birds in.

e4487b61234edfb3.text: What it is for. A sensory exploration of what happens beneath our feet. Children dig gently, smell the earth, and discover the hidden world of roots, worms, and soil life. The skill is touching and smelling.

e4c00725aeacdce8.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather.

e4e1632419549a61.text: Nature recycling system. What happens to a leaf after it falls?

e4e20a372310df8c.text: Underground. What is happening under our feet?

e4f31c6a3fc3b4c1.text: How it runs. You start with See your breath. Visible breath is winter's gift. You can see yourself being alive. Let them experiment with long slow breaths vs quick puffs.

e4fbd4eb490ea526.text: Why it matters. Children are told they are alive, but here they can see it and feel it: warm breath, a warm palm, a body that runs like a little furnace even in the cold.

e51920d7fab472ec.text: Why it matters. Seeds are a gentle way into big ideas: potential, patience, and the future hidden inside small things. Holding an acorn and picturing an oak stretches a child's imagination and their sense of time.

e62bff550ac15e48.text: Before you go out. One thing to gather. Choose a time when the school is quieter (not during break time). The contrast matters.

e6bb7aee1a805452.text: Seed searchers. How does each seed travel?

e6d6ce26725ad41e.text: Then Listen. Do the minute yourself, visibly. The quiet lasts longer if you are in it too. Then listen again in a second spot: near the hedge sounds different from the middle of the field.

e729c0f942b4385a.text: Before you go out. Three things to gather. Glue sticks and A5 paper in a bag. One sheet per child, plus a few spares.

e75b70feff9ad972.text: Then Introduce. No wrong answers. If nobody says the trees, point at one. Keep it simple: after a leaf falls it slowly breaks down, with help from some friendly garden creatures. Worms, woodlice, centipedes. They eat parts of the leaf.

e7ba6729cb3b0745.text: Then Find the warm thing. A wall, a stone, a fence post, dark bark. Compare warm surfaces to cool shaded ones.

e7e050c5993ed370.text: How it runs. You start with Find a bird. Robins, pigeons, crows, sparrows, blue tits. They're here all winter. That takes something.

e7ef286780edd21a.text: Then Wonder. Some kids find this comforting, some find it strange. The land doesn't need us. It does its own thing.

e804a1c7d8935463.text: Footprints. Who has been here before us?

e8b5849fa02fa296.text: Then Wonder. Dormancy is not death. The buds are already there, tiny and waiting. Point one out if you see one.

e8bbd5eceff6b547.text: What it is for. Investigate how plants make their seeds, and discuss how seeds travel to new places and grow into new plants. The skill is wondering how.

e8bdb5956f04ce5a.text: Then Take a rubbing. Hand out paper and crayons at the trees, not before: paper in the hand turns walkers into runners. Pairs work well, one holds the paper flat, one rubs, then swap. Slow strokes beat hard pressing: say "gently, like stroking a cat."

e9008724dc2832cb.text: Why it matters. Sorting is the start of thinking like a scientist. Making the mask puts leaves in their hands. Telling the story puts the animal in their words.

e92ab9b5751ef6b0.text: Why it matters. Pollinators like bees, butterflies and hoverflies are in decline because there are fewer wildflowers than there used to be. Schools have green space that could host wildflowers — this session turns children into tiny conservationists who understand WHY flowers matter.

e9356f534eef702a.text: Why it matters. For young children, a leaf is a first, holdable piece of a tree. Meeting leaves up close, and hearing oak, maple and birch said out loud beside them, is the beginning of knowing the trees in their own grounds by name.

e95123e690e684d8.text: Bulbs. What is being stored away for next year?

e9dc05cf1aeba806.text: And finish in Circle. Describe it: size, colour, where it was. A tree, a flower, food for something. Optional. Beautiful question for the right class.

e9f795cb60ac51f8.text: And finish in Circle. We borrow, we look, we give back. The whole lesson in one move. Woodlice, worms, slugs, and the fungus threads. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer. Everything that ever fell here, all the way down.

ea260a4769c16aa9.text: And finish in Circle. Compare across the group. Different eyes see different things. Encourage precise description. Pollination, survival, evolution in kid-friendly language.

ea5024f759f080a9.text: The idea to carry. Before paint came in tubes, people made their own from plants, berries, soil and rocks. Crushed petals give pinks. Grass gives green. Mud gives brown. Children discover nature's colours with their hands — no brushes, just fingers on paper.

eb7416ed60ceda96.text: How it runs. You start with Trace the sun's path. Summer days are long. The sun travels a huge arc. Let them trace it with their arm.

eb78f83af38de656.text: Blossom. What does opening feel like?

ec8cbfa58e39c68a.text: Then Thank the light. Walk back. Maybe notice which direction home is from here.

ece2eb93a17b0f19.text: What it is for. Choose the class's own tree, greet it properly, and begin a friendship that can last all year. The skill is greeting and returning.

ed579c00902f310e.text: Animal leaf masks. Which animal will you be, and what is its story?

ee2394541f10a271.text: The idea to carry. A seed is a small, quiet package with a whole plant folded inside it, waiting. Dandelion fluff, acorns, grass seeds, the pips in a berry: each one carries the next generation.

ee2f4243381b4049.text: Bare. What can you see now the leaves are gone?

eecf3aced8e6cb5e.text: Then Tell the flower. Say it seriously. The kids will giggle, then some will mean it. Walk back.

eef0ba852317317e.text: What it is for. The closing practice of autumn. Children search for the last warm spots before winter arrives (sun-warmed surfaces, sheltered corners) and say goodbye to the warmth. The skill is noticing by touching.

eefd7cf197e6c734.text: And finish in Circle. Let a few children share with the whole circle. A feather, a seed, a fallen leaf. Hard cases make the best thinking. No right answer. Big guesses welcome.

effa56c4de528a2b.text: Then Wish them well. Walk away quietly so as not to disturb.

f02e86fac248ed43.text: How it runs. You start with Watch the colours turn. Green is leaving. Yellow, orange, red, brown are arriving. Let them catalogue the transition.

f071d11a4c836919.text: Then Count the living. Without moving their feet. Crouch, reach, look closely. Life is everywhere.

f1200ede4178b833.text: And finish with Our autumn garden. The display is the pack's public artefact: drawings, observations, leaves, photographs and the children's own words, each with its finder's name. It tells visiting parents what happened here better than any summary.

f1842ea187584498.text: Then See. Encourage children to look up, down, under...

f26dca9f66ef0799.text: Why it matters. Looking closely is a skill, and a flower is the perfect place to practise it. Children discover that bright colour is not just pretty, it has a job: to be seen by insects.

f2c55acf01d18b7d.text: How it runs. You start with Count everything alive. Grass blades count. Ants count. Moss counts. Bacteria in the soil count (if they think of it). The number will be enormous.

f2df2a2da9a5af03.text: Then Feel the ground. Roots, worms, stones, moisture. Everything counts.

f4019b76fb496a69.text: Then The season in our own words. Three questions is plenty; let answers breathe rather than chasing all of them around the whole circle. The people question is the one this whole pack was for.

f429c0f06ffdd15c.text: Then Wonder. Help them imagine being the animal. Empathy through imagination.

f4554d23258e2114.text: And finish with Circle and feedback. Introduce the idea of nature's recycling system: the leaf falls, the creatures break it down, the soil gets the goodness, a new plant grows.

f51731046294f0d1.text: The idea to carry. Near the end of winter, the first small signs of spring appear. A bud on a twig swells and softens, a snowdrop pushes up through cold soil, the mornings grow a little lighter, and the birds sing louder.

f54c8f1146dc6c9b.text: And finish in Circle. Let students describe textures and discoveries. Encourage imagination: roots growing, worms tunneling. Optional. For reflective classes.

f56a0d00c077a852.text: And finish in Circle time. Keep the masks. They can come out again whenever an animal turns up in a lesson.

f59e94330e0db722.text: Then Discuss. Discussion: how can we as humans help spread seeds and why is it important to have a diverse range of wildflowers? More kinds of flowers means more kinds of pollinators, which means a healthier ecosystem.

f5e1141ff704b2c8.text: What it is for. About using natural resources to create. The skill is looking, touching and smelling.

f66227a2eb96399f.text: And finish in Circle. Share numbers. It's always more than expected. Celebrate the tiny. Close the season with this. Sit with the feeling.

f880e3a405699a2f.text: And finish in Circle. Close by naming what you saw: "I noticed people touching first and looking second. That's how you get to know a tree." If rubbings are damp, they flatten nicely under a book overnight.

f88df382bb625144.text: The idea to carry. Children use paper and crayons to take rubbings from different tree trunks around the school grounds, then compare the patterns. Indoors first: what does bark feel like, is every tree's the same, and how a rubbing works.

f98f72af06ecd766.text: Why it matters. Saying thank you out loud to a living thing feels strange at first and then quietly powerful. Gratitude, spoken and specific, deepens the bond children have been building with the outdoors all term.

f9df0758693ac8dc.text: Then Your winter outside. Gather their answers into the real list as they come: food, water, shelter, warmth, safety. Write or chant it back. Every animal in the garden is solving exactly this list right now, and now the class owns the problem.

fa3ef0ab54822e7c.text: Flowers. What can you see inside a flower?

fa8016c3902c4538.text: Rain. Where has this water been, and where next?

fa89b419b730731d.text: And finish in Circle. Buds, snowdrops, birdsong, longer days. Relief, excitement, hope. Full circle. Close winter, open spring. The year turns.

fa89ea51919f55f8.text: How it runs. You start with Spot a new green. This is a perception exercise. Most kids will say 3-4, then start finding 10, 15, 20 variations.

fa9e8149756f2887.text: The builders. Who is building a home here?

fc2ed31f4d714cf8.text: How it runs. You start with Find who's been here. Mud and frost show tracks. Bird feet, dog paws, fox prints if you're lucky. Even snail trails.

fc303213979c88cd.text: Bird watching. Which birds live here in winter?

fca0524913363ace.text: What it is for. The soundscape narrows. Children listen for what's missing (fewer birds, fewer insects) and discover that in the quiet, deeper sounds emerge. The skill is noticing by listening.

fcea38a7e89663cb.text: The idea to carry. Children find a flying insect, a bee, a butterfly, or a hoverfly, and follow it slowly as it moves from flower to flower. Without ever needing the word pollination, they watch it happen.

fd2f920a98c8f4de.text: And finish in Circle. Size, weight and shape.

fd2fb7d7ca5c7185.text: How it runs. You start with Find a flyer. Sit or stand near flowers. Be patient. Movement will come.

fd3f7de0807feade.text: How it runs. You start with Settle. Give this longer than feels comfortable. A class goes quiet on its own once it is hunting for a sound, and the quiet you wait for lasts longer than the quiet you ask for. Say this one clearly.

fd6bb079675095fa.text: And finish in Circle. Let them argue it out. The wings usually win, but a berry a bird carries goes further than any of them. Any guess counts as thinking like a scientist. No right answer.

fe894643e84cfec5.text: Then Introduce. Conkers come from horse chestnut trees. Acorns come from oak trees. Pass one of each round if you have them.

ff1a9140d339ce33.text: Then Wonder. Some kids will say excited or happy. Others might feel nothing yet. All fine.

ff46eb5dfe1b0438.text: The idea to carry. Spring is building season. Birds gather twigs and moss for nests, insects spin webs, and many creatures fix up shelters for the young ones coming.

ff5d483d02aa7f4f.text: What it is for. Summer has the strongest scents. Children explore smell as the most memory-linked sense: crushing leaves, sniffing bark, getting close to flowers. The skill is smelling and touching.

ff619c54dcf655bb.text: The idea to carry. Spring is when plants open. Tight buds unfold into leaves, flowers spread their petals, and even cracks in the pavement fill with new green.

ffbb7791e7f13a0d.text: Then Touch what grew. Taller plants, thicker branches, new growth. Evidence of time passing.
